tool.name: KernelDensityProportion
tool.summary: Converts a kernel-density raster into a proportion-under-the-surface (volume) raster, where each cell holds the cumulative proportion of the total volume under the surface -- from about 0 at the outer edge to 1 at the peak.
tool.usage:
The "volume" under a kernel density surface is the sum of all cell values (the cell area is constant, so it cancels out of every proportion). For each cell, this tool reports the share of that total volume contributed by all cells whose density is less than or equal to the cell's own density. The result runs from about 0 at the outermost (lowest-density) boundary up to 1.0 at the peak, so it is oriented like the raw kernel density but rescaled to the range 0 to 1.
The proportion surface is designed to be contoured. To draw the X percent home-range isopleth, contour the surface at the value (1 - X/100): for example, contour at 0.05 for the 95 percent isopleth, or at 0.50 for the 50 percent isopleth. The Kernel Density Probability Contours tool recognizes a proportion surface automatically (by a marker written into its metadata) and contours the standard isopleth levels for you.
The output raster stays in the same coordinate system as the source raster; the tool does not honor the Output Coordinate System or other analysis environments, because it transforms the input grid cell-for-cell. Zero and NoData cells of the input are excluded.
The output carries statistics and a histogram so it renders correctly without a separate Calculate Statistics step.

dialogReference.para: A kernel density (or any positive intensity) raster to convert. Cell values are treated as density; zero and NoData cells are excluded from the volume.
The output proportion-under-the-surface raster (values 0 to 1). A suggested name is filled in from the input raster. The output is in the same coordinate system as the input.

Whether the raster's cell values are Densities or Expected counts. This row appears only for a latitude/longitude raster, whose cells narrow toward the poles: a densities raster has each cell weighted by its true area when the volume under the surface is added up, while an expected-counts raster already includes the areas. The value is read from the raster's metadata (Kernel Density Enhanced records what it wrote; Esri's Kernel Density records its choice in the geoprocessing history). When the metadata does not say, Densities is assumed and a warning is shown. On a projected raster every cell has the same area and the setting is not needed.

scriptExample.title: KernelDensityProportion example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Convert a kernel density raster to a proportion surface, then contour it at 0.05 for the 95 percent home-range isopleth.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.KernelDensityProportion( in_raster=r"C:\Project\HomeRange.gdb\KD_density", out_raster=r"C:\Project\HomeRange.gdb\KD_proportion")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Converts a kernel-density raster into a proportion-under-the-surface (volume) raster, ready for contouring into home-range isopleths.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Converts a kernel-density raster into a proportion-under-the-surface (volume) raster: each cell holds the cumulative proportion of the total volume under the surface, from about 0 at the outer boundary to 1.0 at the peak. Contour the result at one minus a target percentage to obtain home-range isopleths (for example, contour at 0.05 for the 95 percent isopleth). Volume is the sum of cell densities (constant cell area cancels); zero and NoData cells are excluded. The output remains in the source coordinate system.
